title: The Invisible Workforce: Domestic Workers Still Lack Protection
title_zh: 看不见的劳动者：家政工人依然缺乏保障
source_name: UN News / Four in five domestic workers lack formal job protections, UN finds
summary_zh: 国际劳工组织（ILO）10 月 27 日发布新报告：2025 年全球约有 8000 万名家政工人，其中约 6650 万人（超过五分之四）属于非正规就业，缺少劳动合同和社会保障。他们的平均月薪只有其他雇员的一半左右，而且很多人工作时间过长。报告还指出，家政工人中女性占 77% 以上。本文适合练习雅思写作中“工作与社会公平”类话题的词汇和数据描述。
paragraphs: Every day, millions of people clean homes, cook meals, look after children and care for older relatives in other people's houses. Without them, many families could not go to work. Yet, according to a new report from the International Labour Organization (ILO), most of these domestic workers have almost no legal protection.

The report, released in Geneva on 27 October, estimates that there were 80 million domestic workers worldwide in 2025, up from 75.6 million in 2019. However, the sector's share of total employment stayed at around 2.2 per cent, which suggests that the rise simply reflects growth in overall employment. The more worrying figure is that about 66.5 million of these workers, or more than four out of five, were informally employed. This means they often have no written contract, no sick pay and no pension, and they are more than twice as likely as other employees to lack effective protection.

The situation varies from region to region. About half of all domestic workers live in Asia and the Pacific. Africa has seen the largest increase since 2019, with an extra 4.2 million people joining the sector, and 93.3 per cent of domestic workers there are informally employed. Even in Europe and Central Asia, where the rate is lowest, more than one in three are paid informally.

Low pay is another serious problem. On average, domestic workers earn just over half of what other employees receive each month, and the gap has been widening since 2019. Working hours are also extreme in both directions. More than a third work at least 49 hours a week, and nearly 15 per cent work 60 hours or more. At the same time, others work short hours for little money and have to move between several households to make a living.

The issue also has a clear gender dimension: women make up 77.2 per cent of domestic workers. Sahra Razavi, an ILO director, said these workers "make millions of lives possible", but their contribution is often taken for granted and undervalued. Experts argue that governments should extend labour laws to cover domestic work, so that the people who care for our families receive fair wages and basic rights in return.
